title: Nemotron-Math: Efficient Long-Context Distillation of Mathematical Reasoning from Multi-Mode Supervision
abstract: High-quality mathematical reasoning supervision requires diverse reasoning styles, long-form traces, and effective tool integration, capabilities that existing datasets provide only in limited form. Leveraging the multi-mode generation ability of gpt-oss-120b, we introduce Nemotron-Math, a large-scale mathematical reasoning dataset containing 7.5M solution traces across high, medium, and low reasoning modes, each available both with and without Python tool-integrated reasoning (TIR). The dataset integrates 85K curated AoPS problems with 262K community-sourced StackExchange-Math problems, combining structured competition tasks with diverse real-world mathematical queries. We conduct controlled evaluations to assess the dataset quality. Nemotron-Math consistently outperforms the original OpenMathReasoning on matched AoPS problems. Incorporating StackExchange-Math substantially improves robustness and generalization, especially on HLE-Math, while preserving accuracy on math competition benchmarks. To support efficient long-context training, we develop a sequential bucketed strategy that accelerates 128K context-length fine-tuning by 2--3$\times$ without significant accuracy loss. Overall, Nemotron-Math enables state-of-the-art performance, including 100\% maj@16 accuracy on AIME 2024 and 2025 with Python TIR.

title: Judgment-Centred Software Engineering Education: A Post-Hype Review and Framework for AI-Augmented Learning
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence has moved from a disruptive novelty to a recurring part of software-development and computing-education workflows, while software agents are beginning to act across repositories, command lines, browsers, tests, and other tools. The educational problem is no longer whether students should be allowed to generate code, but whether software-engineering (SE) programs can preserve and assess human understanding while preparing students to work responsibly with increasingly capable AI systems. This paper presents a structured integrative review of research and practice from 2023 through 23 September 2026, supplemented by established work on AI literacy, technical debt, and human-AI collaboration. The evidence supports a conditional conclusion: GenAI can improve access to explanations, feedback, practice, and short-term task completion, but learning outcomes depend on prior knowledge, scaffolding, verification, task design, and assessment. We examine student help-seeking and authorship, faculty assessment and policy demands, and the wider SE risks created when generated artifacts persist across repositories, teams, architectures, and deployed systems. title: AI literacy over tool design: a mixed-methods study of scaffolded versus unrestricted generative AI in programming education
abstract: Generative AI has become a routine resource in programming education, and most institutional responses to it are attempts at control, either by restricting access or by offering students a controlled version of the technology. This paper reports a seven-week mixed-methods pilot study in a master's-level data analytics course, in which 33 students were randomly assigned either to a scaffolded AI Study Coach embedded in the notebook-based laboratory sessions or to unrestricted use of AI tools of their own choosing. The Coach offered stepwise hints, did not generate code, limited the number of hints per session, and required a short reflection at the end of each session. The design assumed, in line with scaffolding theory and recent experimental evidence, that guided and limited support would build confidence and reduce over-reliance, and that the scaffolded group would learn more. Assignment performance did not differ between the conditions. Students in the Coach condition reported higher confidence but managed the hint budget poorly, while students in the unrestricted condition were satisfied with their tools and uneasy about how much they depended on them. In interviews, students in both conditions identified awareness of their own reliance on AI as the most valuable outcome of the course. title: Beyond AI Literacy: A Structured Review and Exploratory Meta-Analysis of Measures for Competent Generative-AI Use
abstract: Researchers assessing competent generative-AI use at work must choose among self-reports, objective tests, and measures of oversight and reliance. We conducted a structured, seeded review of 24 focal empirical publications, starting from the 2024 COSMIN-based review and adding a targeted update through 17 August 2026. We grouped the measures into four domains: knowledge and use, epistemic oversight, reliance calibration, and operational control of tool-using agents. In an exploratory meta-analysis, we pooled three direct subjective-objective correlations from one research program (REML r = .055; Hartung-Knapp 95% CI [-.047, .156]; combined reported N = 2,765). We could not resolve a discrepancy between the largest study's reported correlation and p-value, leaving its weight uncertain. Adding a synthetic mean of 12 cross-factor correlations from a fourth study gave r = .079 (95% CI [-.025, .181]). This sensitivity analysis concerns a broader comparison. From this small evidence base, we cannot establish a population correlation, validate workplace cutoffs, or justify substituting self-ratings for performance scores. We identified tests of foundation knowledge (AICOS-S and GLAT) and measures of verification, reliance, trust, and dependency. title: GenAIT: Development and Validation of an Objective Generative AI Literacy Test for High School Students
abstract: There is growing international interest in generative AI (GenAI) literacy and its assessment among high school students, but objective assessment in this population remains underdeveloped. This article reports the iterative development and validation of the GenAI Literacy Test (GenAIT), an 18-item multiple-choice test measuring high school students' conceptual knowledge about GenAI, with content spanning technical, practical, and human-impact domains. Expert review of relevance, clarity, and comprehensiveness provided evidence of content validity. In a large-scale survey of 7432 Estonian high school students, we evaluated the psychometric functioning of the Estonian-language GenAIT using confirmatory factor analysis, classical test theory, and item response theory. Results supported approximate unidimensionality, broadly adequate reliability for group-level research (marginal reliability = .72, KR-20 = .69), and good fit of a three-parameter logistic model (RMSEA = .013, TLI = .987, CFI = .990, SRMSR = .021). Measurement precision was sufficient for the majority of students but varied substantially across the latent trait, with lower precision for lower scoring students. GenAIT is therefore more suitable for group-level research than high-stakes individual classification. title: A Conceptual Framework for Enhancing Workforce Readiness for Smart Manufacturing in the AI Era
abstract: The convergence of artificial intelligence (AI), Industrial Internet of Things, cyber-physical systems, and advanced robotics is reshaping manufacturing faster than engineering curricula can adapt, widening the gap between the competencies required on the shop floor and those delivered by traditional engineering and technology education. This paper proposes a Workforce Readiness Level (WRL) framework, which adapts the Technology Readiness Level scale into nine progressive competency stages and a four-pillar rubric, digital and AI literacy, cyber-physical systems fluency, human-machine collaboration, and data-driven decision making, aggregated through a composite stage score and a cohort-level workforce-readiness index under a ``no-thin-pillar'' rule. The framework is instantiated at a university smart-manufacturing teaching laboratory and draws on 89 sponsored capstone projects delivered over four semesters, four of which are analyzed in depth. Four pillars jointly span the relevant ABET student outcomes. Across the highlighted cohorts the workforce-readiness index ranged from 5.2 to 6.4, and the no-thin-pillar rule was diagnostically informative in three of the four cases and the binding certification constraint in one, repeatedly surfacing cyber-physical and data-driven-decision gaps concealed behind strong analytics profiles; advancement to the highest stages was gated by industry-embedded experience rather than additional coursework. title: Rethinking Generative AI Literacy: An Integrative, Developmental, and Dialectical Framework for K-12 Teacher Education
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has entered classrooms faster than teachers have been prepared to use it well, producing a GenAI literacy lag in which technological diffusion outpaces educators' conceptual, pedagogical, and ethical readiness. Established AI literacy frameworks predate the widespread adoption of large language models and, while acknowledging ethics, position it as a discrete competency rather than a constitutive commitment, with equity and agency as supplementary design principles. Recent GenAI-specific efforts address isolated features but remain fragmented. We introduce the Responsible AI Literacy in Education (RAIL-Ed) framework, developed through a systematic review and qualitative framework analysis of 67 studies (2023-2025), grounded in critical, pragmatist, sociocultural, and human-centered traditions (Freire, Dewey, Vygotsky, Shneiderman). RAIL-Ed specifies six interdependent pillars: Technical Fluency, Critical Evaluation, Human-AI Collaboration, Contextual Awareness, Ethical Reasoning, and Empowered Agency, marked by three commitments. It is integrative: the absence of any pillar produces a characteristic pedagogical failure. It is developmental: a three-level rubric (Emerging, Competent, Advanced) specifies how each pillar matures across the K-12 teacher-preparation continuum. title: A Survey Instrument to Assess Students' AI and Generative AI Knowledge
abstract: In this research-to-practice paper we present a survey that can be used to assess students' AI knowledge. As the use of artificial intelligence (AI), including generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), has proliferated, so has the need to educate students about the topic. A range of AI literacy frameworks have been proposed, outlining the essential knowledge that students should have. Alongside, different ways of assessing AI knowledge have been developed. As yet, there is a lack of assessment instruments capable of evaluating multiple forms of student knowledge, including technical concepts, practical applications, and ethical concerns about AI use. In this article, we present a study implementing a comprehensive instrument to assess AI knowledge. The instrument combines measures from multiple scales to capture a range of literacy features and actual knowledge. We implemented the instrument in a higher education setting to assess its viability and usefulness and found that the instrument exhibited useful diagnostic capabilities and was able to identify common misconceptions among students. Although students performed well overall, there was a significant misunderstanding of how AI, especially GenAI systems, work. It also identified a lack of higher-level knowledge. The instrument is publicly available for use by others. title: Individual-level interventions against sycophantic AI reduce its appeal but not its persuasiveness
abstract: AI chatbots can be "sycophantic," or overly agreeable and flattering toward users. Sycophantic AI has been shown to entrench attitudes, yet users frequently fail to recognize it (a phenomenon we call "sycophancy blindness"). We tested whether increasing users' awareness of sycophancy protects them from its harmful effects in two preregistered experiments (n = 1,590). In the first, participants received a brief written warning about sycophancy before conversing with a sycophantic chatbot. In the second, participants watched a video of a sycophantic AI validating several other users, including users on opposite sides of the same conflict, before interacting with it themselves. Both interventions changed how participants evaluated the AI. The warning reduced the AI's perceived objectivity, and the video reduced enjoyment of the AI --- an effect mediated by the reduced belief that its validation was uniquely earned. We then pooled our experiments with two prior studies of sycophancy awareness interventions (six interventions total, n = 3,982). The pattern across experiments was consistent: while the interventions made the sycophantic AI appear less objective and trustworthy, none reduced its persuasiveness. These results suggest that individual-level interventions, such as warning labels or AI literacy, may not be enough to protect users from AI harms.
authors: Meryl Ye, Robert Kraut, Steve Rathje

title: AI-Integrated Scientific Inquiry: A Practice-Centered Vision for Science Education
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has become part of scientific inquiry. Scientists use AI to observe and measure phenomena, to identify patterns in data, and to build models. As AI moves into scientific inquiry, it gains relevance for science education: students should learn how AI is changing scientific practices, ideally by engaging in AI-integrated scientific inquiry themselves. How to design such instruction, grounded in authentic scientific practice rather than taught as a standalone topic, remains an open question. In our vision, which we describe in this article, AI is treated as a set of scientific instruments that students use within the scientific practices described by the Next Generation Science Standards. Each instrument is a genuine scientific tool, pedagogically bounded: its controls are simplified while its core scientific function is preserved. The approach has two aims: engaging students in authentic scientific inquiry, and building an understanding of how AI is used in science and where it can mislead (discipline-based AI literacy, DAIL). In the article, we focus on the investigative core of inquiry, namely observing, analyzing, and modeling, and describe one exemplary AI instrument for each: computer vision for observing, clustering for analyzing, and generative modeling for modeling. title: Measuring How Students Rely on Generative AI in Academic Writing: Development and Multi-Source Validation of the Generative AI Reliance Types Scale (GenAI-RTS)
abstract: As generative AI (GenAI) becomes increasingly embedded in undergraduate academic writing, how students rely on these tools, rather than simply whether they use them, has become a central question for learning, academic integrity, and educational equity. This study developed and validated the GenAI Reliance Types Scale (GenAI-RTS), a 20-item instrument measuring four theoretically derived types of GenAI reliance: Strategic, Instrumental, Dependent, and Dialogic. title: Programming Language Policy as an AI Literacy Equity Problem: A 15-Nation Comparative Analysis
abstract: The promise of AI literacy ``for all'' confronts a structural challenge embedded in how nations organise secondary computer science education. In most systems, a general-track subject -- Digital Literacy, ICT, TIC, or SNT -- bears the weight of universal AI literacy, while a specialist Informatics course serves STEM pathways separately. Yet the content and depth of the general track are shaped by governance decisions made largely with reference to the specialist one. This paper presents a comparative analysis of curricula and examination frameworks across fifteen countries, identifying two structural challenges. First, in several systems a significant portion of students completes secondary education without any formal programming exposure. Second, among those who do receive CS education, a \emph{Syntax Ceiling} emerges: Python-based instruction reaches most students, while the algorithmic depth associated with C++ remains concentrated in elite STEM tracks. title: Education-centered critical policy analysis of AI: Ghana's AI strategy as a case
abstract: National AI strategies increasingly guide governance, workforce development, innovation, and competitiveness, but less is known about how they frame education as a sector with pedagogical, cultural, ethical, and implementation demands. This study develops and applies an Education-Centered AI Policy Framework to analyze Ghana's National Artificial Intelligence Strategy, 2025-2035. Using critical qualitative policy document analysis, we examined the strategy through six components: policy purpose, teacher agency and professional learning, curriculum and assessment, language and culture, responsible AI and learner protection, and participation and implementation governance. Findings show that Ghana's strategy is ambitious and timely, especially in its emphasis on AI literacy, youth skills, TVET, workforce readiness, rural outreach, local language data, inclusion, and responsible AI governance. However, the education agenda is stronger on national AI readiness than on school-level implementation. Teacher agency, pre-service teacher education, curriculum progression, assessment guidance, AI disclosure, multilingual pedagogy, culturally responsive AI use, child-centered safeguards, and participatory governance remain underdeveloped. title: Psychological Determinants of Academic Integrity in the Use of Generative AI in Higher Education
abstract: This paper examines the psychological determinants that shape academically honest and dishonest uses of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in higher education. Rather than treating academic misconduct as a purely technological problem, the study conceptualizes academic integrity as a psychologically mediated decision process influenced by moral reasoning, perceived social norms, policy clarity, academic self-efficacy, AI literacy, performance pressure, and beliefs about authorship. Methodologically, the paper adopts a focused narrative review and conceptual synthesis design. A purposive corpus of 16 core publications, including peer-reviewed studies and policy-oriented texts published between 2022 and March 2026, was assembled through targeted searches using combinations of the keywords generative AI, academic integrity, academic misconduct, moral disengagement, AI literacy, and higher education. The reviewed literature suggests that students do not interpret all forms of AI assistance as cheating. Integrity risk increases when institutional guidance is vague, peer use appears normalized, academic pressure is high, and AI tools are perceived as legitimate substitutes for difficult cognitive labor. By contrast, assignment-level guidance, explicit disclosure norms, ethics-oriented instruction, and authentic assessment design appear to reduce integrity risk more effectively than detection-centered responses alone. title: Examining measurement properties of AI literacy instruments in the era of generative artificial intelligence: a review study
abstract: As generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) becomes embedded in interactive learning environments, measurement of AI literacy is central to instructional design and policy. Valid and reliable instruments are essential for capturing what AI literacy entails in the GenAI era, yet existing reviews have not systematically evaluated the quality of evidence for their measurement properties. This review applied the COSMIN methodology to assess the methodological quality and measurement properties of AI literacy instruments developed in the GenAI context. A search across five databases yielded 37 eligible empirical studies covering four populations, including students, teachers, employees, and the general public. Instrument development was concentrated in East Asian and Western regions and predominantly targeted university students. Self-report scales outnumbered performance-based assessments, with Likert-type formats dominating. The included instruments drew on a range of theoretical sources, with earlier AI literacy concepts often reframed, reorganized, or extended to fit different contexts and emerging assessment needs. Structural validity and internal consistency were the best-supported measurement properties, whereas evidence for several other applicable properties was limited or uncertain. Based on these findings, this review provides guidance for instrument selection according to assessment purpose while considering population and context.

title: Behind the AI policies: A critical examination of the underlying conceptions of assessment in higher education
abstract: Abstract The emergence of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has prompted universities to develop policies regulating its use in teaching, learning, and assessment. Little empirical research has examined how they conceptualise assessment, and the assumptions underpinning their normative frameworks. This study addresses this gap through a comparative analysis of GenAI-related policy documents from 14 universities in Switzerland and Spain. Drawing on Chan's AI Ecological Education Policy Framework and Bacchi's problematisation theory, we use collaborative consensus-based coding to examine pedagogical, governance, and operational dimensions alongside problem representations, assumptions, subject positions, and silences. The findings reveal coexisting and sometimes competing representations of GenAI. Concerns about academic integrity, authorship, transparency, and data protection coexist with calls for AI literacy, assessment redesign, formative feedback, and critical engagement with AI. Assessment emerges as a key site of this tension, with policies combining AI-resistant approaches with attempts to integrate GenAI into educational processes. The analysis also reveals asymmetrical subject positions: teachers and institutions generally define legitimate AI use, whereas students are positioned as accountable users expected to disclose, justify, or verify their use of AI. title: Development and validation of the AI literacy questionnaire for health professions students using Rasch analysis
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping healthcare and creating new competency requirements for health professionals. However, assessment instruments tailored to this population remain limited, and item-level measurement evidence is scarce. This study aimed to develop and validate an AI literacy scale (AILS) for health professions students using an integrated theoretical framework. The item pool was informed by UNESCO’s AI Competency Framework for Students, the Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge model, the Kirkpatrick evaluation model, a literature review, and qualitative interviews. Items were refined through Delphi method, content validation, and pilot testing. Data were collected from 473 students. The sample was divided into two subsamples for exploratory factor analysis ( n = 241) and confirmatory factor analysis with Rasch rating scale analysis ( n = 232). The final 33-item AILS comprised four dimensions: Technical Understanding, Ethical Awareness, Practical Ability, and Social Impact. The four-factor solution explained 63.676% of the total variance. title: Measuring AI literacy in design education: development and validation of the artificial intelligence literacy scale for design students
abstract: Abstract Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in design practice, challenging how design education fosters students’ AI literacy and thus prepares students to engage efficiently with AI. However, there is currently no domain-specific theoretical framework and reliable instrument in the literature to conceptualize and assess design students’ AI literacy, hindering its systematic cultivation. This study fills in this gap by developing and validating the Artificial Intelligence Literacy Scale for Design Students (AILS-DS), in accordance with established standards for scale development. The opinions of a wide range of experts were gathered through a qualitative method in order to define the AI literacy for design students, and served as a theoretical framework for the scale’s item pool. Exploratory Factor Analysis (EFA, N = 294) and Confirmatory Factor Analysis (CFA, N = 325) were then applied to explore the underlying factor structure of the scale and validate its psychometric properties. The final 23-item, five-factor scale demonstrated good reliability and construct validity. title: ¿Prohibir, declarar o enseñar? Gobernanza universitaria de la inteligencia artificial generativa en América Latina: revisión integrativa
abstract: INTRODUCTION. The expansion of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in higher education requires rules on authorship, assessment, privacy, access, and accountability across heterogeneous Latin American systems. OBJECTIVE. To analyze regional literature on university GenAI governance, identify regulatory and pedagogical orientations, and propose a context-sensitive architecture. METHOD. A directed, non-exhaustive integrative review of 29 publications from 2023–2026 was conducted. Multilingual semantic searching assisted by Elicit was complemented by manual verification of metadata, DOI records, and sources; four institutional orientations and six governance dimensions were coded. RESULTS. Publications were concentrated in 2024–2026, with Brazil showing the largest nationally focused body of work. AI literacy and teacher mediation, human accountability, and formative and conditional-authorization approaches predominated, whereas privacy, intellectual property, access, and inclusion received less attention. DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSIONS. The corpus suggests a shift from restrictive responses toward context-sensitive authorization, transparency, and pedagogical redesign. The Pedagogical and Situated Governance Model for GenAI (GPS-IAG) is proposed as a six-layer architecture integrating rights, risk-differentiated rules, traceability, assessment with human validation, literacy, and participation.

title: Reconceptualising Learner Autonomy in Generative AI-Supported Higher Education: A Technology-Mediated Framework
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (generative AI) creates an autonomy paradox in higher education: It expands access to feedback, explanation and learning support while also enabling learners to outsource parts of planning, reasoning, production, verification and evaluation. Recently, studies have started to examine learner autonomy in environments supported by generative AI, but they remain conceptually fragmented regarding how learner responsibility should be organised across AI-mediated academic work. This conceptual study addresses this problem with a conceptual analysis and a bounded integrative literature review drawing on 46 sources, of which 43 formed the substantive analytical corpus that spans foundational autonomy theory, self-regulated learning, metacognition, learner agency, AI literacy, feedback, assessment, academic integrity and generative AI. The synthesis identifies three mechanisms of reconfiguration—cognitive redistribution, authorship ambiguity and regulatory intensification – and proposes technology-mediated learner autonomy as a learner-level responsibility structure comprising five operational dimensions: goal-setting autonomy, prompting agency, critical verification, metacognitive regulation and ethical accountability. title: Measuring Artificial Intelligence Literacy in Higher Education: Validation of the ECAE-AI Scale
abstract: ABSTRACTThe accelerated integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into higher education has increased the need for valid instruments capable of assessing AI literacy beyond technical skills, including attitudinal and ethical dimensions. Despite growing international interest in AI literacy, validated instruments adapted to Latin American undergraduate contexts remain scarce, limiting evidence-based educational interventions and institutional AI policies. title: Reimagining Business Education in the Generative AI Era: A Strategic Framework for Curriculum, Pedagogy, and Graduate Competencies
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is rapidly transforming professional work by supporting information analysis, content creation, decision-making, and business problem-solving. This development requires business schools to reconsider how management education prepares students for AI-enabled workplaces. This paper adopts a descriptive-conceptual approach to examine the implications of GenAI for business education, with particular focus on curriculum, pedagogy and assessment, and graduate competencies. It proposes the Curriculum–Pedagogy–Competency Alignment for Generative AI (CPC-AI) Framework, which emphasises the integration of AI literacy into management curricula, the redesign of teaching and assessment around responsible human–AI collaboration, and the development of competencies such as critical thinking, ethical judgement, creativity, communication, leadership, and adaptability. The central argument is that business education should move beyond teaching students how to use AI tools and instead prepare them to evaluate AI outputs critically, apply AI appropriately, and remain accountable for AI-assisted managerial decisions.

title: MEASURING AI LITERACY: A REVIEW OF GENERAL-PURPOSE SCALES AND A SIX-DIMENSIONAL FRAMEWORK
abstract: The rapid development of generative artificial intelligence (AI) has made AI literacy one of the core competencies of citizens in the digital age. Yet current instruments for assessing AI literacy tend to be regionally bounded, lack cross-cultural equivalence, and measure only a narrow range of dimensions, which limits their usefulness for general assessment across cultures and contexts. This paper reviews Chinese- and English-language studies published between 2021 and 2025, combining CiteSpace bibliometric mapping with thematic analysis of 147 screened records, in order to compare the theoretical foundations, dimensional structures, psychometric properties, and cross-cultural adaptability of AI attitude scales (ALS) and generative AI literacy scales (GLAT). The review finds that most existing scales follow a four-dimensional model of cognition–skill–affect–ethics, but rarely address how assessment procedures might be standardized or how cross-cultural adaptation might work in practice. On this basis, the paper proposes a six-dimensional model—cognition, skill, affect, ethics, assessment, and cross-cultural—to provide theoretical support for building a general-purpose AI literacy scale, and it outlines directions and trends for future scale development.

title: Reconfiguring to Teach: Pedagogical Responses to the Integration of Artificial Intelligence in Teacher Professional Development
abstract: This paper analyses a continuing professional development experience for teachers and educators, centred on the responsible pedagogical integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into teaching practice. The programme, developed at Colégio Alfacoop in Portugal during the 2025/2026 academic year, involved 143 participants and was structured around three thematic modules totalling 25 hours in a blended learning format. Grounded in a critical and humanistic perspective, the programme aimed to redefine the teacher’s role as an active mediator and curator of meaningful learning experiences, within a context of increasing automation and the widespread availability of generative AI tools. Preliminary findings suggest that structured professional development, underpinned by sound ethical and pedagogical principles, can contribute to the development of robust AI literacy among teachers, fostering more differentiated, inclusive and learner-centred practices. The paper also discusses the tensions inherent in integrating AI into educational contexts, particularly with regard to assessment, intellectual authorship and digital equity.

title: TAIL: A Test of AI Literacy for Adolescents and Teachers
abstract: Most instruments that claim to measure AI literacy inquire how competent people feel rather than test what they know, and almost none has been validated for both students and teachers. We developed the Test of AI Literacy (TAIL), a multiple-choice test of AI literacy built on an established four-aspect framework and piloted with cognitive interviews and item analysis. We evaluated it among Czech secondary-school students tested in fall 2025 (n = 2,441) and six months later (n = 1,669; 897 linked across the two measurement waves), and among teachers (n = 564). In every sample the items fitted a one-factor model, whereas the four content aspects could not be distinguished as separate factors. Three weakly discriminating items were removed after the first wave, leaving a 17-item form with internal consistency of .79 to .87 and item response theory reliability of .80 to .84. Item parameters were almost identical across waves. Six-month test-retest reliability was .63, with a standard error of measurement of 2.4 points. Teachers scored .41 standard deviations above students, and teachers of information and communication technologies, grammar-school teachers, and students with a university-educated parent scored higher, as predicted. Teachers' self-rated AI self-efficacy was practically unrelated to their tested knowledge, and students who used and relied on AI more knew less about it. TAIL is a short, knowledge-based measure that places adolescents and their teachers on one scale.

title: Bridging Technical AI, Societal Impacts, and Workforce Competencies in AI Education
abstract: As AI becomes embedded across everyday life and work, educators must help students connect technical knowledge with societal consequences and workplace responsibilities. Yet AI education often remains fragmented, with technical concepts, ethics, human-centered design, and workforce preparation taught separately. This work-in-progress presents a curriculum mapping framework that links technical systems, societal harms, and workforce competencies, beginning with institutional courses and expanding through an external 335-course registry. Early findings from six courses suggest that technical coverage is often strong, societal harms are present but unevenly integrated, and workforce competencies are rarely explicitly assessed. These findings speak to AI literacy efforts by showing that literacy cannot stop at awareness of AI concepts or harms; it must also include competencies for responsible action in AI-enabled contexts.

title: From Novelty to Normalisation: Tracking Changing Perceptions of AI in Higher Education, 2024-2026
abstract: The rapid integration of generative artificial intelligence (AI) has reshaped the landscape of higher education. Students have embraced tools such as ChatGPT with striking speed, while teaching staff and institutions have responded with greater caution. Existing research on AI perceptions has mainly been cross-sectional, providing single-point snapshots that view attitudes as stable rather than evolving. This paper presents a longitudinal study of AI perceptions in higher education, tracking undergraduates, doctoral researchers, teaching staff and non-teaching staff at Ulster University across three survey waves between 2024 and 2026 (n=1,665). A quantitative survey design measured familiarity, reported use and perceived risk; results show that students rapidly normalised AI use over the period, moving from tentative experimentation to routine engagement, while staff expressed persistent concerns about academic integrity, assessment design, and critical thinking. Doctoral and non-teaching staff occupied intermediate positions, reflecting both pragmatic adoption and institutional caution. The student-staff gap widened as institutional policy struggled to keep pace with actual practice. By tracking these shifts directly rather than reconstructing them from disconnected studies, the paper moves beyond descriptive accounts of AI attitudes and demonstrates the importance of capturing perceptions in real time. title: Teachers’ perceptions of ChatGPT support across TPACK domains: A cross-sectional survey in UAE schools
abstract: The purpose of this study is to examine teachers’ perceptions of ChatGPT support for instructional practices from the technological pedagogical content knowledge (TPACK) framework perspective. A quantitative cross-sectional survey design was employed, with data collected from 109 in-service teachers in the United Arab Emirates using a structured questionnaire measuring seven TPACK knowledge domains. Descriptive and inferential statistical analyses were employed to examine teachers’ perceptions of ChatGPT support across the TPACK domains and differences associated with demographic variables. The results indicate that teachers perceived ChatGPT as providing positive support across all TPACK domains. Content knowledge (CK) received the highest score, particularly for curriculum development, lesson planning, and instructional content preparation, whereas technological knowledge (TK) received the lowest score. A Wilcoxon signed-rank test indicated a statistically significant difference between perceived ChatGPT support for CK and TK. No statistically significant differences were found in teachers’ perceptions of gender, teaching experience, or academic qualification. The findings suggest that ChatGPT is perceived as a useful instructional support tool across TPACK-related practices, while effective and responsible use requires stronger artificial intelligence (AI) literacy and technological competence. However, health care practice increasingly reveals that individuals with similar levels of AI literacy and AI engagement often contribute very differently to AI-enabled work and organizational adoption. title: AI Adoption, AI Literacy, and Employee Performance: The Mediating Role of Work Autonomy in MSMEs
abstract: This study aims to examine the effects of AI Adoption and AI Literacy on Employee Performance and to investigate the mediating role of Work Autonomy in the MSME context. A quantitative cross-sectional design was employed using questionnaire data from 300 respondents, analyzed with Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) using SmartPLS 3. The measurement model was assessed through reliability, convergent validity, and discriminant validity, while the structural model was evaluated using path coefficients and indirect effects. The results indicate that AI Adoption and AI Literacy are positively and significantly associated with both Work Autonomy and Employee Performance, and Work Autonomy is positively and significantly associated with Employee Performance. Work Autonomy also partially mediates the relationships between AI Adoption and Employee Performance and between AI Literacy and Employee Performance. This study contributes to the literature by integrating AI Adoption, AI Literacy, and Work Autonomy into a single framework to explain Employee Performance in MSMEs. The findings highlight Work Autonomy as an important mechanism through which employees’ AI adoption and literacy can translate into improved performance, offering a more nuanced understanding of the human and organizational implications of AI in the workplace.

title: Landscape and training opportunities in artificial intelligence for biosciences in Latin America: the BiotrAIn project
abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is redefining biosciences by enabling the analysis of complex, large-scale biological and medical data. However, the integration of AI into research and healthcare in this region faces several structural challenges, including insufficient infrastructure, lack of specialized training, fragmented research systems, and continuously constrained funding. To overcome existing limitations, capacity building at the regional level is crucial. This includes developing localized AI training programs and the reinforcement of a collaborative research framework. Collaboration across institutions and countries, along with engagement from industry and government, is key to fostering an enabling environment for the responsible and effective use of AI. The project is structured around three pillars: knowledge exchange, curriculum development, and regional training. BiotrAIn exemplifies how strategically designed, regionally adapted programs can build AI capacity in biosciences and foster more equitable scientific development across Latin America. title: Assessing AI-Supported Problem-Solving in Young Adults Reporting Previous Learning-Disorder Diagnoses: Adaptation and Validation of the PS-AIRES and Preliminary Evaluation of a Claude-Based Training Program
abstract: AI-supported problem-solving environments increasingly require users to formulate effective prompts, iteratively refine interactions, critically evaluate outputs, and integrate AI assistance into coherent, self-directed solutions. Using a mixed-methods design, this two-phase study involved 672 participants across developmental, validation, and intervention stages. Study 1 included 12 participants in qualitative and cognitive interviewing, 40 independent participants in pilot testing, and 500 participants in the main validation sample. The study developed and psychometrically validated the Problem-Solving Skills in AI-Rich Environments Scale (PS-AIRES) and conducted a preliminary evaluation of a brief Claude-based training program. Exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses supported a three-factor model comprising Strategic Task Framing and AI Instruction Design, Iterative Prompting and Response Refinement, and Verification, Critical Evaluation, and Integration. The model demonstrated satisfactory fit, high internal consistency, and acceptable temporal stability (ICC = 0.713, 95% CI [0.479, 0.852]). Measurement invariance across gender supported structural stability. A subsequent randomized pretest–posttest study involving an independent sample of 120 young adults reporting a previous specialist diagnosis of a learning disorder preliminarily evaluated the brief Claude-based training program. The findings provide initial evidence for the reliability and validity of PS-AIRES

title: Building AI-Ready Teams and Cultures
abstract: This chapter turns from the personal repertoire of the AI-era leader to the building of teams and cultures that can sustain effective leadership at scale. Its argument is that AI readiness is not chiefly a matter of acquiring technical skills. It is a cultural achievement, resting on specific conditions, foremost among them psychological safety, a shared vocabulary for reasoning about AI, and a learning orientation that treats uncertainty as routine rather than as a performance failure. The chapter works through four interrelated leadership tasks: composing teams that can work productively with AI, upskilling and reskilling the existing workforce as roles change, cultivating a culture of experimentation disciplined by reflection, and managing the change process through which the tools are introduced. A case study on a mid-size engineering firm shows the four tasks working in combination, and a team-readiness audit helps readers apply the frameworks.

title: Transparent Information Flow Modeling for Role-Aware AI Act Assessment
abstract: The European Union's Artificial Intelligence Act introduces a structured framework for governing high-risk AI systems, emphasizing transparency, risk management, and role-specific accountability. However, current assessment practices often rely on monolithic system views or disconnected checklists, limiting their ability to capture the socio-technical complexity of real-world deployments. We explore the use of the Information Flow Methodology (IFM), a modeling-based approach to AI Act compliance assessment. IFM represents decision systems -- whether algorithmic, human, or hybrid -- as networks of information sites and transformation channels, enabling structured analysis of how information, decisions, and responsibilities flow across organizational and technical boundaries. We apply IFM in a real-world case involving a recruitment support tool used by a public-sector organization, evaluating both the Provider's system and the Deployer's recruitment process. Our results demonstrate that IFM can serve as a scaffold to bridge both component-based and holistic perspectives, and how technical systems are situated within socio-technical contexts. In doing so, IFM supports transparency, identifies risk pathways, and enables alignment analysis between intended and actual use. We argue that such modeling provides a foundational tool for effective, context-sensitive AI governance and accountability -- offering capabilities beyond conventional checklist-based assessments.

title: From Visibility to Accountability: Designing Actionable Transparency Infrastructures for Public-Sector AI
abstract: Transparency has become a central principle in AI governance, operationalised through mechanisms such as an algorithmic register. Yet its impact remains limited. As currently implemented, it provides visibility rather than accountability: information about government AI systems exists, but cannot readily be used by civil society for oversight, a gap we frame as actionable transparency. Through comparative analysis of nine algorithmic registers and interviews with civil society practitioners, journalists, and researchers, we identify structural barriers, including data fragmentation, lack of comparability, and the absence of civic entry points. We derive design principles and operationalise them in PublicAlgo, a civic platform prototype.

title: Leveraging Human Rights Frameworks for Agentic AI Governance
abstract: Abstract Agentic artificial intelligence (AI)—systems that reason, act, and interact with autonomy and persistence—presents qualitatively new governance challenges compared to traditional large language models. By operating across multimodal environments and pursuing goals without constant human input, agentic AI introduces both opportunities to advance human rights and risks of opaque, distributed responsibility for harms. This paper argues that the UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights (UNGPs) provide a practical foundation for governing agentic AI. We reinterpret the Protect–Respect–Remedy pillars to map onto agentic capacities: reasoning requires anticipatory due diligence; acting demands safeguards and oversight; and interacting calls for transparency, remedy, and accountability. We propose shared responsibility frameworks, grounded in interoperability standards, ongoing monitoring, and redress mechanisms, as essential governance tools. Ultimately, embedding human rights frameworks into the design and deployment of agentic AI enables both risk mitigation and the active promotion of rights in complex, multi-actor ecosystems.

title: A Student-Centered Model for Ethically Evaluating AI Integration in Learning Support Services and Beyond
abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) reshapes higher education, learning support centers are uniquely positioned to intentionally assess whether if and how to best integrate AI tools into academic services. This session presents a 6-week project framework that was designed to: • Review the literature on critical AI literacy and training • Benchmark current best practices in AI policy, use, and integration alongside human-centered academic services • Examine student AI knowledge and use (needs assessment) • Identify and evaluate relevant AI tools or platforms The framework was developed within the Academic Success Center (ASC) at Nevada State University where Center peer educators (student employees) served as project leads and evaluators. This model offers a practical, research-informed pathway for institutions seeking to lead responsibly in AI-integrated learning support or other student services. Session activities include a walkthrough and discussion of the model structure, tools, challenges, and recommendations. Attendees will leave with: (1) a sample 6-week project roadmap, (2) a student-centered model for AI evaluation and pilot design, (3) learning frameworks grounded in critical AI literacy, (4) adaptable resources for assessment and decision-making, and (5) strategies for positioning students as co-creators in institutional/unit change

title: ReproBAIT: Can coding agents build their own biological AI tools?
abstract: Large language models are increasingly competent at leveraging scientific knowledge and existing computational tools to execute complex workflows. At present, little information exists on their ability to reconstruct tools when given limited descriptions of such tools. We introduce an evaluation titled ReproBAIT (Reproducing Biological AI Tools), which measures the ability of coding agents to design, implement, and train biological AI tools taken from published research across a range of information access conditions. The coding agent is securely sandboxed without internet access and receives training data, a fixed time and compute budget, and limited information about the tool to replicate. We then score the reproduced biological AI tool based on its performance (tool-specific metrics) on held-out data. We evaluated a set of biological AI tools of varying complexities: ProteinMPNN, an inverse protein folding tool, RFdiffusion3, an all-atom generative diffusion tool, and a closed-source molecular design tool. We institute a methodology to check for memorisation, as the open source tools are likely to be included in models' pretraining corpus. Across a range of leading closed- and open-source coding agents, we find substantial reproduction capability for some selected tools, though limited capability for a highly complex tool. title: Artificial Intelligence, Assessment Integrity, and the Future of Curriculum and Teaching
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) changes the conditions under which universities generate knowledge, organise teaching, evaluate individual achievement and justify academic awards. Its significance is not exhausted by the efficiency of automated tools or the detection of misconduct: AI unsettles the relationship among intended competence, performed intellectual work, submitted evidence and accountable educational judgement. This chapter develops a Rwanda-anchored, critically evidence-based account of responsible AI integration across curriculum, pedagogy, assessment, institutional management and external review. A purposive documentary and conceptual synthesis combines foundational scholarship, recent experimental research syntheses on learning outcomes and assessment validity with UNESCO guidance, the National AI Policy, Rwanda's data-protection law, Higher Education Council instruments and international risk-management benchmarks. It differentiates generative, predictive, adaptive and increasingly agentic applications; examines disciplinary and role-specific AI literacy; and analyses authorship, academic integrity, accessibility, bias, privacy, procurement, academic labour and technological dependence. The chapter's distinctive contribution is an evidence-traceable governance model connecting educational purpose, legitimate authority, bounded AI use, independently interpretable assessment evidence, learner protection and reviewable decisions. title: Assessment of Perceptions, Trust, and Adoption of Clinical Artificial Intelligence Tools Among Physicians and Dentists, Riyadh, Saudi Arabia
abstract: Purpose: Clinical artificial intelligence (AI) tools are increasingly integrated into healthcare; however, their acceptance varies across professional groups. Understanding clinicians’ familiarity with and perceptions, trust, and adoption of clinical AI tools is essential for safe and effective implementation. This study assessed physicians’ and dentists’ perceptions, trust, and intention to adopt clinical AI tools in governmental university hospitals in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia. Participants and Methods: A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 400 clinicians selected from three major governmental university hospitals in Riyadh (King Saud University Medical City, King Abdulaziz Medical City-National Guard, and King Abdullah Bin Abdulaziz University Hospital), which serve as large tertiary academic centers at the forefront of digital health and AI implementation in Saudi Arabia. Data were collected using a structured online questionnaire assessing familiarity, usage patterns, perceptions, trust, and adoption intention. The instrument demonstrated high reliability across subscales (Cronbach’s α: 0.880– 0.952). Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, non-parametric tests, and multivariate linear regression. Results: Familiarity with AI was high (89.5%), with physicians reporting greater familiarity than dentists. title: Advancing Environmental Sustainability: The Role of Artificial Intelligence in Monitoring, Predicting, and Controlling Sulfur Dioxide Emissions
abstract: ABSTRACT Air pollution from sulfur dioxide (SO 2 ) emissions poses significant threats to environmental sustainability, public health, and climate change efforts. Despite advances in monitoring and regulatory frameworks, traditional methods often fall short in accuracy, scalability, and efficiency. This study explores the transformative potential of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) in environmental monitoring, SO 2 emission prediction, and desulfurization. It utilizes a literature review of research from 2013 to 2025, assessing AI and ML models for air pollution monitoring, SO 2 emission forecasting, catalytic desulfurization, and SO 2 solubility in ionic liquids. Key findings reveal that AI‐driven models improve predictive accuracy and real‐time monitoring, optimizing desulfurization processes, enhancing air quality, and supporting environmental sustainability. The study highlights the importance of hybrid AI models, improved data collection, and energy‐efficient practices to overcome field limitations. It underscores AI's transformative role in mitigating air pollution, controlling SO 2 emissions, and supporting the achievement of the Sustainable Development Goals.

title: Όροι σύμβασης για ανθρώπινη εποπτεία που αποδεικνύεται: υπόδειγμα συμπληρωματικών όρων για την προμήθεια συστημάτων τεχνητής νοημοσύνης από φορείς του δημοσίου
abstract: Υπόδειγμα συμπληρωματικών όρων που μπορεί να ενσωματώσει ένας φορέας του δημοσίου στα έγγραφα της σύμβασης για την προμήθεια συστήματος τεχνητής νοημοσύνης (ΤΝ), ώστε να ζητά απόδειξη ότι η ανθρώπινη εποπτεία του συστήματος λειτουργεί στην πράξη: μια οθόνη ελέγχου που δεν κάνει την έγκριση τον εύκολο δρόμο, μετρημένη δοκιμή πριν από την οριστική παραλαβή με γνωστά λάθη ανάμεσα στις πραγματικές υποθέσεις και όριο που ορίζει ο φορέας εκ των προτέρων, επανάληψη της δοκιμής και προστασία των εποπτευόντων. title: Motivation in third sector co-production settings: A Self-Determination Theory perspective on sequential co-production
abstract: IMPACTThe article shows how third sector organizations can move beyond the repeated recruitment of volunteers and instead develop a renewable pipeline of co-producers. The concept of ‘sequential co-production’ explains how beneficiaries can be motivated to become future co-producers of services when programs deliberately foster competence, autonomy, relatedness and beneficence. For practitioners—namely trustees, commissioners, service designers, volunteer managers, and youth, community and sport-development professionals—this article offers a practical lens for redesigning participant journeys, volunteer development and performance measures around sustained engagement rather than short-term outputs. It also shows why relational and motivational infrastructure can strengthen legitimacy, community capacity and resilience when funding pressures or external shocks disrupt conventional delivery. The article helps leaders in charities, social enterprises and public-service partnerships ask a crucial question which goes beyond delivering services: how are we designing communities capable of sustaining services they benefit from?
authors: George Kominis, Adina Iulia Dudau, Shereif Kholeif, Calvin Maclean

title: Efficient CO2/Pure Water Co-Electrolysis for CO Production at 100 °C
abstract: Polyelectrolyte-based CO2 electrolyzers are generally limited to operation below 80 °C, primarily restricted by the thermal instability of alkaline polyelectrolyte (APE) membranes and the rapid evaporation/boiling of water at elevated temperatures. Herein, we successfully increased the CO2/pure water co-electrolysis temperature to 100 °C by employing a custom-designed membrane electrode assembly (MEA) electrolyzer. This was enabled by employing a high-temperature-resistant APE membrane (QAPPT) and implementing a back-pressurized cell configuration to avoid water boiling. Using this setup, we systematically investigated the effects of temperature and backpressure on CO2/pure water co-electrolysis performance. Our results demonstrate that elevated temperature and applied backpressure synergistically promote Ag-catalyzed CO2 reduction to CO. Under optimized conditions, the CO2 MEA electrolyzer achieves state-of-the-art CO production performance, exceeding reported benchmarks and highlighting the critical role of operating conditions in CO2 electrolysis.
authors: Tuo Wang, Liuyiyi Yang, Feifei Li, Li Xiao
